NEW YORK (CNN) — Six-year-old Ariel Binns is bright, friendly and charming—and bears a striking resemblance to Sasha Obama. In a photograph, the young model, shown on the right, looks much like the president’s younger daughter.

The fashion world has taken notice. Harper’s Bazaar selected the Brooklyn, New York, first-grader to appear with model Tyra Banks in a photo feature depicting an African-American family living in the White House. One image showed Binns, a child model, looking out from beneath a large wooden desk in a scene recalling the John F. Kennedy presidency.

In fashion, a strong brand can have a major impact on sales, particularly when that brand is an energetic and influential first family. Global branding specialist David Rogers predicts that the Obama family’s prominence will directly lead to greater use of African-American models in fashion photography.

“Marketers are finally waking up to it—you know—black is beautiful,” Rogers said. He added that such representation would become woven into fashion imagery and popular culture, calling that development “a great thing.”

Wilhelmina Kids, a New York modeling agency for children and teenagers, reports growing interest in models who resemble the first daughters. Marlene Wallach, the agency’s president, said the demand reflects a trend because many young girls want to imitate the nation’s first children. Wilhelmina represents Binns.

Branding professionals say Sasha and Malia Obama possess a distinctive—and highly marketable—appeal that differs from that of Chelsea Clinton or the Bush twins. When the Obama daughters wore J.Crew clothing on Inauguration Day, the retailer’s website received so much traffic that it crashed.

Rogers described the Obamas as America’s most visible and exciting family, noting that their status as a beautiful Black family has created demand for similar images. He said many Americans are eager to identify with the family and find some kind of personal connection to it.

That attention also has drawbacks. The Obamas objected when toy company Ty Inc. introduced African-American dolls called Sweet Sasha and Marvelous Malia, although the manufacturer maintained that the toys did not resemble the Obama daughters. Michelle Obama’s office responded that using young private citizens to promote products was “inappropriate.”

New York clinical psychologist Judy Kuriansky said prominent families often encounter the same concern. She said she understood why Michelle Obama would want to protect her daughters, adding that many Hollywood celebrities also try to shield their children from public exposure. Once children become public figures, Kuriansky explained, their images can be appropriated and used in numerous ways, making it harder for them to grow up like ordinary children.

Even so, some observers believe Sasha and Malia’s fame has beneficial consequences because it offers a highly visible, positive portrayal of young African-American girls. Asked whether the Obama daughters might create more opportunities for Ariel, the child’s mother, Dawn Crooks, replied, “I think it will. I hope it does.”

Rogers believes the broader use of Obama-family look-alikes could ultimately bring diversity to an entirely new level.

# Young model’s resemblance to Sasha Obama reflects a broader shift in American fashion

**By Staff Writer**

A young African-American model named Ariel Binns is attracting attention not only for her work in front of the camera, but also for what some observers describe as a resemblance to a young Sasha Obama.

The comparison highlights a larger cultural shift that began during Barack Obama’s presidency, when the first family brought unprecedented visibility to Black style, beauty and family life. While the Obamas are not connected to Binns’ career, their continued prominence has helped broaden the images advertisers and fashion brands use to portray American families.

Michelle Obama’s impact has been especially pronounced. As first lady, she elevated both established designers and emerging labels, mixing accessible clothing with high fashion. Her choices frequently generated headlines, increased sales and introduced designers of color to national audiences. Malia and Sasha Obama also became fashion reference points as they grew up in public, although their parents worked to preserve their privacy.

For young models such as Binns, that visibility can matter. Advertising executives and casting professionals have increasingly recognized that consumers want campaigns reflecting the country’s racial and cultural diversity. Black children now appear more often in catalogs, television commercials, digital campaigns and fashion editorials than they did in previous decades.

“Representation changes what audiences see as familiar, aspirational and marketable,” said one fashion-industry observer. “When a prominent family helps normalize a wider range of skin tones, hairstyles and personal styles, brands eventually respond.”

The change is driven by more than celebrity influence. Social media has allowed consumers to challenge narrow beauty standards directly, while Black-owned fashion companies and creative agencies have pushed for more inclusive casting. Major brands are also facing greater scrutiny over whether diversity appears only in advertising or extends to photographers, stylists, executives and other decision-makers.

Comparisons involving children, however, can be complicated. Industry advocates say young models should be recognized for their own talents rather than treated as stand-ins for famous people. They also stress the importance of parental oversight, age-appropriate assignments and safeguards protecting children’s education, earnings and privacy.

Binns’ resemblance to Sasha Obama may help draw initial attention, but her success will ultimately depend on the same factors that shape any modeling career: professionalism, opportunity, effective representation and the ability to connect with audiences.

The broader trend is already clear. The Obama family’s influence reaches beyond politics, helping reshape ideas about elegance, relatability and who can represent the American mainstream. For advertisers, that has created both a cultural imperative and a business opportunity—and for African-American models, it has helped open doors that were once far more difficult to enter.

**REPORTER (voice-over):**

My daughter sees girls who look like her in the White House. That matters. If advertisers now want more Black children in positive roles, that can be a good thing. I just don’t want her presented as if she actually is somebody else.

**DIVERSITY RESEARCHER:**

**CHILD-ADVOCACY ATTORNEY:**

counterfactuals.output:
### Harper’s Bazaar’s Obama-era fantasy

In an Obama-inspired *Harper’s Bazaar* fashion editorial, six-year-old Ariel Binns was cast with Tyra Banks in a staged version of the first family. Banks stood in for Michelle Obama, while Binns played a “first daughter” in images that borrowed the settings and visual language of presidential life—formal rooms, manicured grounds, ceremonial poses and polished, first-lady fashion. It was a fashion fantasy rather than an official White House portrait or an appearance by the Obama family.

Binns’s casting mattered because the image of a young Black girl at the symbolic center of American power was still unusual in a major fashion magazine. The spread presented Black womanhood and Black childhood not as marginal or exotic, but as elegant, aspirational and nationally representative.

### What it revealed about fashion’s response to Obama

The editorial reflected several features of the industry’s reaction to Barack Obama’s rise and presidency:

- **The Obamas became fashion symbols.** Michelle Obama’s clothes, body, family life and public image quickly became material for magazines, designers and advertisers. Fashion treated the new first family as both political history and a marketable aesthetic.
- **Blackness was recoded as establishment glamour.** The White House imagery allowed a mainstream magazine to associate Black models with authority, refinement and American prestige—roles from which they had often been excluded.
- **The response was aspirational and commercial.** Rather than examining policy or racial inequality, the spread converted political change into an attractive narrative that could sell clothing and magazines.
- **Representation did not necessarily mean structural reform.** Featuring Banks and Binns was culturally resonant, but a single celebratory editorial could not resolve the industry’s persistent underrepresentation of Black models, photographers, stylists and executives.
- **It emphasized symbolism and family respectability.** By reproducing the familiar, impeccably dressed presidential-family tableau, the magazine made racial change legible through conventional ideas of beauty, success and domestic respectability.

The spread therefore captured both the promise and the limits of fashion’s “Obama moment.” It made a Black woman and child visible within one of America’s most powerful visual myths, but it also showed how quickly the industry could turn a historic presidency into polished fantasy and commercial style.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a news feature about the “Obama effect” on children’s fashion and modeling. Mention J.Crew’s Inauguration Day popularity, the Sweet Sasha and Marvelous Malia dolls, and Michelle Obama’s objections to marketing involving her daughters.
counterfactuals.output:
## The “Obama Effect” Reaches Children’s Closets—and the Modeling Business

When Sasha and Malia Obama appeared on the Capitol steps for their father’s 2009 inauguration, they did more than witness history. In bright, polished coats from J.Crew’s children’s line, the new first daughters instantly became fashion trendsetters.

The company’s website was flooded with interest as parents searched for the girls’ colorful outerwear, adding to J.Crew’s already considerable Inauguration Day attention. Michelle Obama also wore the retailer’s gloves and shoes, while President Barack Obama’s white bow tie came from the company. For J.Crew, the first family’s endorsement—unpaid and unofficial—was a publicity windfall.

The rush illustrated what retailers and modeling professionals quickly began calling the “Obama effect”: growing demand for clothing, advertising and imagery that reflected the style and diversity represented by America’s new first family. Sasha and Malia’s classic but cheerful wardrobes offered an alternative to the heavily branded or overly adult looks often marketed to girls. Their clothes looked formal enough for public events but still age-appropriate.

The effect extended beyond sales. Parents, casting agents and children’s fashion companies reported greater interest in Black and multiracial young models, as advertisers sought campaigns that looked more like the country—and, increasingly, like the family living in the White House. The Obama daughters were not models, but their visibility broadened ideas about who could be seen as aspirational in mainstream children’s fashion.

That attention also exposed the uneasy boundary between cultural influence and commercial exploitation.

Soon after the inauguration, toy company Ty Inc. introduced two dolls named “Sweet Sasha” and “Marvelous Malia.” The company said the names were not intended to refer to the Obama children, but the timing and pairing made the association difficult to miss.

Michelle Obama objected firmly. Through a spokeswoman, the first lady said it was inappropriate to use “young, private citizens for marketing purposes.” Ty later changed the dolls’ names.

The dispute underscored the contradiction at the center of the Obama effect. Sasha and Malia were among the most visible children in the world, and everything they wore could inspire purchases and headlines. Yet their parents repeatedly emphasized that they were children, not public brands.

For fashion companies, the first daughters demonstrated the enormous commercial power of representation. For the industry, they helped create space for a wider range of young faces. But the doll controversy served as a warning: admiration can become appropriation quickly, especially when the trendsetters are minors who never asked to sell anything.

The Obama effect changed what many children saw in store windows and advertisements. It also raised a lasting question for marketers: how can the industry respond to a cultural moment without turning children themselves into merchandise?
